route: Bounded width: a seventh polynomial class, or the exact place where interface tables explode
headline: Both halves settled. NEGATIVE: the exact-table dynamic programme over a decomposition explodes already at treewidth 3 / pathwidth 4 -- thm:fold's P_D has exactly 2^{(N-2)/6} response pieces with tw(P_D)=pw(P_D)=4 (exact), and the explosion is impossible at interface dimension one (tw:one-live), so the threshold is located exactly. POSITIVE: the SEARCH does not explode. Running the Etessami-Papadimitriou-Rubinstein-Yannakakis Tarski fixed-point search on lem:cut's cut map F_S at every bag of a balanced separator recursion decides SSG-Value on stopping games of treewidth k in 2^{O(k log^2 N)} = N^{O(k log N)} exact arithmetic operations -- QUASIPOLYNOMIAL at every constant width, beating thm:subexp's e^{2 sqrt n} there (flagged as new but a candidate rediscovery; no such algorithm is known to me for quantitative SSG values). The seventh polynomial class is tw:modulator: N^{O(mu)} where mu is the least number of vertices whose FREEZING puts the game in any freezing-closed polynomial class; for P = k-acyclic this answers the question rem:kacyclic explicitly leaves open (what happens when mu_k > 0), and it strictly generalises Auger-Coucheney-Strozecki's feedback-vertex parameter. A companion theorem, poly(N)2^{f_k} where f_k is the number of colour-k vertices on cycles, is also new to the paper. The family M_n (N = 5n+3, two players) has mu_max = 1, feedback vertex number >= n+1, and is OUTSIDE all six existing polynomial classes -- including a clean proof that every escape certificate for it has 1 - lambda < 4*2^{-n}. Validated: 300 stopping SSGs built from random tree decompositions of width <= 3, plus 150 of exact treewidth 3, zero mismatches against brute-force max-min, all in exact rational arithmetic and self-certified by T(w)=w.

results.name: tw:response
results.statement: For a set A of non-terminals with outer boundary dA, the response function R_A(phi) = val of the game on A with dA frozen at phi is monotone; the value is equivariant under an affine change of ALL terminal payoffs, hence 1-Lipschitz in sup norm in the full payoff vector and in any subvector; on stopping games R_A is piecewise affine with at most 2^{|C cap A|} distinct affine pieces, each v_{sigma,tau}(phi) = sum_w h_{sigma,tau}(v,w) phi_w with h the first-passage law, and the region where one pair is optimal is a convex polyhedron. The piece number pi(A) is what a table-storing DP must pay.
results.argument: Monotonicity is the first line of lem:cut's proof. Equivariance: max, min and the mean commute with x -> ax+b, so the shifted/scaled operator is conjugate to T and the least fixed points correspond; monotone + shift-equivariant implies nonexpansive. Traps of the frozen game are traps of H, so stopping is inherited (lem:trapchar) and I-P_{sigma,tau} is invertible (lem:denominator), giving affineness by expanding (I-P)^{-1} = sum P^k. thm:stopping-determinacy gives val = max-min of these; lem:local-global cuts the optimality region out by affine inequalities.
results.verification: Exact arithmetic on 400 random stopping games of treewidth <= 3 with random frozen sets |S| <= 4: 1600 monotonicity checks, 1600 sup-norm-Lipschitz checks, 1221 affine-equivariance checks, no failure. (The first version of the claim -- shift-equivariance in the FREE coordinates alone -- was REFUTED by the test and corrected: t_0, t_1 do not move.)

results.name: tw:fold-width
results.statement: For thm:fold's P_D with A = V minus {u,t0,t1}: the coordinate of R_A at F_D has exactly 2^D = 2^{(|V|-2)/6} affine pieces with breakpoints j*2^{-D}, and pi(A) = 2^D as well. Moreover tw(P_D) = pw(P_D) = 2 for D=1, 3 for D=2,3, and 4 for D=4; pw(P_D) <= 4 for every D by an explicit path decomposition, and pw(P_D) > 3 for 4 <= D <= 8. Hence no bound pi <= poly(N, tw): the exact response tables are 2^{Omega(N)} already at treewidth four.
results.argument: The piece count is thm:fold. The widths: the exact elimination-ordering and vertex-separation subset DPs on Gamma(P_D) (6D vertices) for D <= 3; the layout u, X_1, k_{2D-1}, Y_1, F_1, G_1, (k_{2D-2d+2}, k_{2D-2d+1}, X_d, Y_d, F_d, G_d)_{d=2..D} with bags B_i = {v_i} u (frontier of the prefix) gives width 4 for all D; and an exhaustive search over all layouts/elimination orderings of width 3 finds none for 4 <= D <= 8.
results.verification: thm:fold's identity re-derived in exact arithmetic for D <= 8 at every dyadic grid point, every midpoint and five off-grid rationals, against backward induction, slope set exactly {0, 2^{-D}}; the 2^D optimal pairs on the 2^D intervals are pairwise distinct for D <= 8; the width-4 path decomposition verified as a genuine decomposition for D <= 12 and D = 20,30,45,60.

results.name: tw:one-live
results.statement: Let H be a payoff game with no directed cycle among its non-terminals, z a terminal, Z the set of non-terminals from which z is reachable, and suppose every vertex of Z has AT MOST ONE successor in Z u {z}. Then theta -> val_{H[z:=theta]}(v) is monotone, 1-Lipschitz and piecewise affine with at most |Z|+1 pieces.
results.argument: Each v in Z has exactly one theta-dependent successor w, the other having a constant value c_v; so f_v = op_v(f_w, c_v) with op_v in {max(.,c), min(.,c), (.+c)/2}, each monotone, 1-Lipschitz and adding at most one breakpoint. Induction along a topological order. The point is that every SSG value is NONDECREASING in every other (lem:monotone), so a one-dimensional interface transports a composition of monotone one-variable maps, whose preimages of a breakpoint are single points: no folding accumulates. thm:fold's fold is exactly a two-dimensional interface -- F_d and G_d read the SAME pair, and max - min = |.| in the difference coordinate.
results.verification: Proof only; the complementary side (2^D at interface dimension two) is tw:fold-width.

results.name: tw:no-clock
results.statement: Let Lambda be a two-input two-output gadget whose internal vertices read no terminal and from each of which an input is reachable. Then Phi(f+c,g+c) = Phi(f,g)+c and Phi(lf,lg) = l*Phi(f,g), so Phi_1 - Phi_2 = psi(f-g) with psi(d) = alpha*d for d >= 0 and beta*|d| for d <= 0; psi^D has at most two affine pieces for every D, and a chain of D copies of Lambda has at most two linearity domains in the initial difference. A fold that accumulates therefore requires the gadget to read a terminal.
results.argument: max, min and the mean commute with x -> x+c and with x -> lx applied to both inputs; Lambda stopping makes the fixed point unique so the conjugated operators have corresponding fixed points. Additive homogeneity gives Phi_i(f,g) = g + Phi_i(f-g,0), positive homogeneity makes psi linear on each half-line through 0, and such maps compose to such maps, so sign(psi^j(d_0)) is determined by sign(d_0).
results.verification: 3000 random acyclic terminal-free gadgets in exact arithmetic: no violation of either identity; the difference map of 400 of them has at most two affine pieces, breaking only at 0. (The stopping hypothesis is necessary and is stated: an internal cycle with no input reachable has lfp value 0, which does not move.)

results.name: tw:cut-sign
results.statement: For a stopping payoff game H and a set S of non-terminals, lem:cut's cut map F_S satisfies: H[x] is stopping for every x; val_H|_S is the UNIQUE fixed point of F_S; and F_S(x) <= x implies x >= val_H|_S, while F_S(x) >= x implies x <= val_H|_S.
results.argument: A trap of H[x] avoids the terminals hence avoids S, so it is a trap of H and empty. Assembling x with val_{H[x]} and using eq:assembly turns F_S(x) <= x into T_H xhat <= xhat and F_S(x) >= x into T_H xhat >= xhat; cor:comparison (stopping) gives the two conclusions, and applying both at a fixed point gives uniqueness. This two-sided sign property is contained in lem:cut's proof but not stated there.
results.verification: Exact arithmetic on 400 random stopping games of treewidth <= 3 with random S: 400 checks that val|_S is a fixed point of F_S and 2400 checks of the two sign implications at random grid points; no failure.

results.name: tw:tarski
results.statement: For a finite chain L with M elements and a monotone F: L^d -> L^d, a fixed point is found with at most 2(ceil(log2 M)+1)^d evaluations of F, by: recurse into the (d-1)-dimensional slice at the midpoint m of the last coordinate to get y*; evaluate F at x = (y*, m); if F(x)_d = m return x; if F(x)_d > m recurse on [F(x), hi]; else on [lo, F(x)].
results.argument: Invariant: F maps the box into itself, so Knaster-Tarski gives a fixed point inside; the slice map is monotone into itself, so the recursive call is legitimate and F(x)_{<d} = x_{<d}. If F(x)_d > m then F(x) >= x, so F maps [F(x),hi] into itself; symmetric otherwise. Progress: the new corner has last coordinate >= m+1 (resp. <= m-1), so that range at least halves. Cost recursion Q(d,M) <= (log M + 1)(Q(d-1,M)+1). Using F(x) rather than x as the new corner removes the usual need for the recursive call to return a LEAST fixed point.
results.verification: 400 random monotone maps on boxes of dimension up to 4 and side up to 63: every returned point is a fixed point, mean 13.8 queries; and agreement with exhaustive enumeration of all fixed points on 300 small boxes. (An earlier version that cut at x rather than F(x) was found to LOOP FOREVER on an explicit 4x4 map and was discarded.)

results.name: tw:round + tw:recover
results.statement: For a finite chain L of mesh eps, F^L = roundup_L o F_S is a monotone self-map of L^S and every fixed point thetahat of it satisfies val_H|_S <= thetahat <= val_H|_S + N*2^a*eps. If Delta is a common denominator of H's terminal payoffs, every value of H has denominator dividing an integer <= Q = Delta*2^a, so an approximation within 1/(2Q^2) recovers the exact value by continued fractions.
results.argument: Round-up is monotone; thetahat >= F_S(thetahat) gives thetahat >= val by tw:cut-sign, and thetahat <= F_S(thetahat) + eps assembles to T xhat <= xhat <= T xhat + eps, whence ||xhat - val|| <= sum_k (1-2^{-a})^{floor(k/N)} eps = N 2^a eps by thm:contraction (which holds verbatim for payoff games, lem:gen-comparison). Recovery: Cramer with det A_U <= 2^a (lem:denominator-sharp) and Legendre's convergent theorem.
results.verification: Used inside every run of the algorithm, and every run ends with an exact check T(w) = w; over 300 + 150 + 48 solved games there was no certification retry, so the a-priori precision was always sufficient.

results.name: tw:modulator (with cor tw:kacyclic-mu)
results.statement: Call a class P of payoff games freezing-closed if it is preserved by retyping any set of vertices as terminals with arbitrary payoffs, and let mu_P(G) be the least |X| with G[X:=theta] in P for all theta. If P is freezing-closed and solvable exactly in time p(n,beta), then the value vector of a stopping payoff game G is computed exactly in O((B+2)^{mu} p(n,O(B)) + poly) with B = O(a + log N + log Delta); for an SSG this is N^{O(mu)}p(N,O(N)), polynomial whenever mu = O(1). The k-acyclic classes are freezing-closed and are solvable for arbitrary terminal payoffs (thm:kacyclic), so SSG-Value is decidable in N^{O(mu_k)} -- which answers the question rem:kacyclic explicitly leaves open, and reduces to thm:kacyclic at mu_k = 0.
results.argument: Freeze X at a grid point, solve the residual game in P exactly, apply op_x at each x in X: this evaluates lem:cut's F_X exactly, so the computed map is exactly F_X and monotone. Round up onto the dyadic grid of mesh eps = 1/(4N 2^a Q^2) (tw:round), run tw:tarski in dimension mu, recover exactly (tw:recover), solve once more at the recovered theta for the values off X (lem:cut, last clause), and certify by T_G w = w, which pins the answer because a stopping game has a unique fixed point.
results.verification: Implemented (modulator.py) and run on M_n for 2 <= n <= 12 with X = {h}: 10 or 11 cut-map evaluations, exact value vector, certified by T(w)=w, and cross-checked against brute-force max-min for n <= 4 and against Hoffman-Karp throughout. Also run on P_D^circ for D <= 12 with X = {u}: four evaluations, exact.

results.name: tw:colour-feedback
results.statement: For k in {max,min} let f_k(G) be the number of kind-k vertices lying on a directed cycle. Then the value vector of an ARBITRARY SSG, stopping or not, is computable exactly in time poly(N) 2^{f_k(G)}; polynomial when f_k = O(log N). (Not available for k = avg: a coin cannot be frozen.)
results.argument: Enumerate the 2^{f_k} choices on the set F of kind-k vertices on cycles; retype each v in F as an AVERAGE vertex with both out-edges to the chosen successor, which leaves the operator's value unchanged. No Max vertex of the modified game lies on a cycle -- those of F are no longer Max, those outside F lie on no cycle by the choice of F -- so it is max-acyclic and thm:kacyclic solves it in polynomial time with no stopping hypothesis. Positional determinacy gives val = max over the enumeration (min for k = min), since Max restricted can only lose and equality holds at sigma*|_F.
results.verification: The enumeration agrees with brute-force max-min on 200 instances, both colours, exact arithmetic, no failure. Note mu_k <= f_k always, so tw:modulator applies whenever this does; the two bounds N^{O(mu_k)} and 2^{f_k} are incomparable.

results.name: tw:qp
results.statement: SSG-Value on stopping payoff games given a tree decomposition of width k of the interaction graph is decided EXACTLY with 2^{O(k log^2 n)} = n^{O(k log n)} arithmetic operations on rationals of O(n^{1+log_2 3} + n^{log_2 3} log Delta) bits. In particular any family of treewidth O(1) is decidable in QUASIPOLYNOMIAL time N^{O(log N)}, self-certified by T(w) = w.
results.argument: Balanced-separator recursion. A centroid bag X (|X| <= k+1) leaves components of at most n/2 vertices; each component's successors lie in the component, X or the terminals, so freezing X at theta gives independent stopping subgames of treewidth <= k and half the size, and solving them recursively evaluates lem:cut's F_X exactly at theta. At each node run tw:round + tw:tarski in dimension k+1 over a dyadic grid of B = O(3a + 2 log Delta + log n) bits, then tw:recover. Bit bookkeeping: delta_{j+1} <= 3 delta_j + 4n over log_2 n levels gives O(n^{2.585}) bits. Cost: T(n) <= 2(B+2)^{k+1} * (sum_i T(n_i)) <= n^{O(k)} * 2T(n/2), so T(n) = 2^{O(k log^2 n)}.
results.verification: Implemented (alg.py) in exact rational arithmetic. 300 stopping SSGs built from RANDOM TREE DECOMPOSITIONS of width <= 3 (exact treewidth 1/2/3 on 62/167/41, 30 above the exact-DP budget): 0 mismatches against brute-force max-min, 616773 cut-map queries, maximal Tarski dimension 4, maximal grid 2^100, no certification retry. A second run of 150 games of EXACT treewidth 3 with the base case lowered to three vertices (deepest recursion): 0 mismatches, 62602 queries, grid up to 2^82. Beyond brute-force range, batches of twelve games at 16, 22, 28 and 34 non-sink vertices agree with the independent Hoffman-Karp solver and satisfy T(w) = w. FLAGGED: this is new to my knowledge but a candidate rediscovery; see the literature remark.

results.name: tw:cyclic
results.statement: P_D^circ (P_D with u retyped as an average vertex u -> (F_D, t_1)) is a stopping SSG on 6D+2 vertices with pw <= 5 (tw = pw = 4 at D = 3), every cycle of which meets u; val(u) = 1/2 + 3*2^{-(D+3)} for D >= 2, which lies in the MIDDLE piece (the 2^{D-1}-st of 2^D) of the response function of tw:fold-width. The algorithm of tw:modulator with X = {u} returns the exact value vector after FOUR cut-map evaluations for every 2 <= D <= 12, while the exact table has 2^D pieces.
results.argument: The instance closes thm:fold's fold into a genuine cycle so that the exponential table cannot be side-stepped by choosing the sweep direction (P_D itself is acyclic, so tw:fold-width alone is a statement about tables, not instances). It exhibits the dichotomy of this section on one family: the table is 2^{Omega(N)} and the search is O(1) queries.
results.verification: Exact computation for D <= 12: stopping, freezing u leaves an acyclic game, value formula, piece index, and the query count are all from the exact implementation; the widths are the exact subset DPs at D <= 3 and the explicit decomposition with u added to every bag otherwise.

results.name: tw:family (M_n)
results.statement: M_n (N = 5n+3, a = 3n, |Vmax| = n+1, |Vmin| = n; a Max/Min/avg ring through a Max hub h feeding thm:vi-lower's ratchet G_n) is stopping, fully reachable from h, has mu_max = 1 with X = {h} and feedback vertex number >= n+1, and lies OUTSIDE all six polynomial classes: a = 3(N-3)/5; the ring cycle carries all three kinds so no k-acyclicity holds; H(M_n) is a single SCC on all n+1 Max vertices; val(c_1) = 1/2 + 2^{-(n+1)} and min_j val(c_j) = 2^{-n} so the common denominator is >= 2^{n+1}; d(M_n) >= n; and EVERY escape certificate has 1 - lambda < 4*2^{-n}, so thm:escape-class gives at least a*2^{n-3} rounds. Yet tw:modulator solves it in polynomial time, and val(h) = 1/2 + 2^{-(n+1)} so the threshold is decided by an exponentially small margin.
results.argument: Stopping by peeling the trap from c_{2n} inward. Every cycle through an x_i must run forward through x_{i+1},...,x_n,h and back, so freezing h destroys every Max cycle while the y_i <-> b_i two-cycles and the c-part cycles survive: mu_max = 1 but fvs >= n+1 (n+1 pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles), so the class strictly beats the feedback vertex number. The c-part is successor-closed, so lem:successor-closed + thm:vi-lower give its values. d(M_n) >= n: the levels of lem:descent's filtration are l(c_i) = n-i+1, each c_i (i <= n) has exactly one successor of strictly smaller level, so the descent path c_1 -> ... -> c_n -> t_1 has sum omega = n, for every sigma. Escape: for i < n, (x(c_1)+x(c_{i+1}))/2 <= lambda x(c_i) gives u_{i+1} <= 2 lambda u_i - 1 with u_1 = 1; u_n > 0 forces g(t) := 2t(2-2t)^{n-1} < 1 with t = 1-lambda, and g >= 1 on [4*2^{-n}, 1/2], so t < 4*2^{-n}.
results.verification: Exact solves for n <= 12, cross-checked against brute-force max-min for n <= 4 and certified by T(w) = w; value alphabet n+3 letters and common denominator exactly 2^{n+1}; d(M_n) = n+1 with a unique optimal Max strategy for n <= 7; mu_max = 1 and no feedback vertex set of size <= min(n,5) by exhaustive search; and the exact-arithmetic feasibility test finds NO escape certificate at lambda = 1 - 4*2^{-n} for n = 3,4,5, matching the proved threshold.

results.name: tw:gap2-shape (searches toward GAP 2)
results.statement: For chains of one fixed gadget that may read t_0, the level map in the projective coordinate is a piecewise-Moebius psi(r) = B/(A+B), and GAP 2 asks whether some such psi has an invariant interval carrying two full monotone branches. Two searches say no. (a) Over the closure of {0, f, g} under max/min/mean capped at 260 piecewise-linear functions, all 59315 admissible ordered pairs (A,B): the largest piece count of psi^D for D = 1..9 anywhere is 5,13,23,35,49,65,83,101,119 -- QUADRATIC, against 2^9 = 512. (b) Allowing t_1 as well, so Phi:[0,1]^2 -> [0,1]^2 is a general autonomous monotone nonexpansive PL map, the number of distinct itineraries of Phi^D on an exact 25x25 rational grid SATURATES AT 11 within three steps over 200 random gadgets.
results.argument: Not a proof. Search (a) is exhaustive over a finite closure of gadget outputs but that closure is capped; search (b) is random, which by the standing experience of this project is no evidence at all. Both are reported as measurements, and both are consistent with tw:no-clock's proved statement that a terminal-free chain cannot fold twice.
results.verification: mobsearch.py (exact rational piecewise-Moebius composition, 59315 pairs) and t_2d.py (exact rational grid itineraries, 200 gadgets).

gap:
GAP 1 (the main one). MISSING STATEMENT: "There is an algorithm that computes the value vector of every stopping SSG of treewidth k in time N^{f(k)} for some function f." tw:qp gives N^{O(k log N)}; the loss is exactly the factor 2 per level of the balanced separator recursion, each level re-solving both sides from scratch at every Tarski query, and storing the response function instead of re-querying it is precisely what tw:fold-width forbids (2^{Omega(N)} pieces at treewidth 4).

GAP 2. MISSING STATEMENT: "There is a family of stopping payoff games of pathwidth at most 3, with one free parameter, whose response function has 2^{Omega(N)} affine pieces." tw:fold-width achieves this at pathwidth 4 and tw:one-live forbids it at interface dimension one; tw:no-clock proves that a chain of identical terminal-free gadgets cannot fold twice, and tw:gap2-shape reduces what remains, for chains of one fixed gadget, to: "is there a piecewise-Moebius map psi(r) = Phi_2(1,r)/Phi_1(1,r), with Phi_1, Phi_2 built from max, min, the mean and the constant 0, having a nondegenerate invariant interval J on which psi has two monotone branches each mapping J onto J?"

Two further items are stated but not proved here and should not be cited as established: (i) that no polynomial or quasipolynomial algorithm for the QUANTITATIVE value of bounded-treewidth SSGs exists in the literature -- this is from memory only, and tw:qp is therefore flagged as a candidate rediscovery; (ii) the exact form (FPT vs XP, and the exact parameter) of Auger-Coucheney-Strozecki's almost-acyclic result, also from memory.
next_steps:
1. ATTACK GAP 1 FIRST -- it is the only thing between this route and a genuine seventh polynomial class covering all bounded-width instances. The obstruction is concrete and local: at a separator X the two sides are re-solved from scratch at each of the O(B^{k+1}) queries. Two ideas that do not obviously die: (a) warm-start the child search from the previous query's answer and bound the TOTAL work across a monotone sequence of queries (the Tarski search's queries are not monotone, but the sign-definiteness of tw:cut-sign means each query moves one corner of a shrinking box, so the children are solved on a nested family of payoff vectors -- a potential-function argument on the children might amortise the depth away); (b) replace the balanced separator by a path decomposition and a single left-to-right sweep in which the state is the value vector on one interface, so that the recursion depth is 1 and the cost is (number of interfaces) x (queries) -- this needs the interface fixed point to be solvable without recursion, which is exactly where the response table would be needed, so (a) looks more promising.

2. CHECK THE PRIOR ART. tw:qp is the single claim in this route most likely to be a rediscovery, and I could not check it. Someone with source access should verify: (i) whether any polynomial or quasipolynomial algorithm for SSG values at bounded treewidth is published; (ii) Auger-Coucheney-Strozecki's exact parameter and bound; (iii) whether Etessami-Papadimitriou-Rubinstein-Yannakakis (or Fearnley-Palvolgyi-Savani, Chen-Li) already combine Tarski search with graph decompositions.

3. IMPROVE THE MODULATOR CLASS. mu_P is defined for any freezing-closed P; only P = k-acyclic is instantiated here because thm:kacyclic is the only class in the paper stated for arbitrary terminal payoffs. Restating thm:few-avg, thm:few-escape, thm:escape-class and thm:bounded-components for payoff games would immediately widen the class, and each is a small piece of work. Also: mu_k is computable in N^{O(mu)} by brute force, but a polynomial-time recognition of "mu_k <= c" for fixed c is a separate (standard-looking, FPT-flavoured) question worth settling before the class is quoted as checkable.

4. USE tw:qp AS A DESIGN CONSTRAINT ON THE PIVOT. Every family in the document -- L_n, H_m, G_m, WD, CC, P_D -- has treewidth at most 4, so all of them are quasipolynomial by tw:qp and polynomial by tw:modulator. Any candidate superpolynomial ALL-SWITCHES family (the missing item of the AUSO pivot) that has bounded treewidth is therefore hard for the rule, not for the problem. If the root agent wants an instance that is genuinely hard, tw:qp says it must have treewidth omega(1) -- which is a real, cheap, checkable filter on future constructions and should be applied to G# and to any realisation of thm:blowup's second level.

5. SETTLE GAP 2 by answering the piecewise-Moebius question of tw:gap2-shape (a clean one-dimensional dynamics problem, independent of games), or by an engineered pathwidth-3 fold. Do NOT re-run random searches: the two reported here already say "probably not" and the standing rule is that random sampling is not evidence.

\section{Width, freezing, and the Tarski search}\label{sec:tw}

Every polynomial class of \Cref{sec:special} is a colour condition on cycles
(\Cref{thm:kacyclic}), a count
(\Cref{thm:few-avg,thm:few-escape,thm:bounded-components}), a rate
(\Cref{thm:escape-class}) or the answer
(\Cref{thm:few-denominator}).  None is a \emph{width} condition, and the
hard families of this document are all of small width: the exact values of
$\tw=\pw$ are $2$ for $H_m$ and for $G_m$ of \Cref{thm:vi-lower}, $3$ for
the ladder $L_n$, for $\mathrm{WD}(e,j,m)$ and for $\mathrm{CC}(L,m)$ at
every parameter within reach of the exact dynamic programme, and $4$ for
$P_D$ of \Cref{thm:fold}.  This
section asks what a decomposition buys.  The answer has two halves.  The
table-based dynamic programme, which stores the exact response function of
each part, is \emph{exponential already at pathwidth four}
(\Cref{tw:fold-width}).  The \emph{search}-based algorithm, which never
stores a table and only queries the response at grid points, is
quasipolynomial at every constant width (\Cref{tw:qp}) and polynomial
whenever a bounded set of vertices carries all the recursion
(\Cref{tw:modulator}); the latter answers the question left open in
\Cref{rem:kacyclic}.

Throughout, $H$ is a payoff game in the sense of \Cref{def:payoff}: vertices
of kind $\max$, $\min$, $\mathrm{avg}$ of out-degree two, and terminals of
out-degree zero carrying payoffs in $[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q$.  We write $n$ for
the number of non-terminals, $a$ for the number of average vertices,
$C=\Vmax\cup\Vmin$, and $\val_H=\lfp(T_H)$.

\begin{definition}[The width of a game]\label{tw:width}
The \emph{interaction graph} $\Gamma(H)$ of a payoff game is the undirected
simple graph on the \emph{non-terminal} vertices with an edge $\{u,v\}$
whenever $u\ne v$ and $v$ is a successor of $u$ or $u$ of $v$.  The
treewidth $\tw(H)$ and pathwidth $\pw(H)$ of $H$ are those of $\Gamma(H)$.
Terminals are excluded because they are absorbing and never need to be
separated; including $t_0,t_1$ as vertices raises either parameter by at
most two.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The response function, and why the tables explode}

\begin{definition}[Response function]\label{tw:response-def}
Let $A$ be a set of non-terminals of $H$ and let
$\partial A:=\{w\notin A: w$ is a successor of some $v\in A\}$ be its
\emph{outer boundary} (terminals of $H$ included).  For
$\varphi\in[0,1]^{\partial A}$ let $H_A[\varphi]$ be the payoff game on
$A\cup\partial A$ in which every $w\in\partial A$ is a terminal of payoff
$\varphi_w$; the coordinates of $\varphi$ at the terminals of $H$ are frozen
at their own payoffs, so the free parameters are the non-terminals of
$\partial A$.  Put
\[
  R_A(\varphi)\;:=\;\val_{H_A[\varphi]}\big|_A\;\in\;[0,1]^{A}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[The response function]\label{tw:response}
Let $A\subseteq V\setminus(\text{terminals})$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $R_A$ is monotone; shifting \emph{every} terminal payoff of
      $H_A[\varphi]$ --- the frozen ones and the terminals of $H$ alike ---
      by a constant $c$ shifts $R_A$ by $c$; and consequently $R_A$ is
      $1$-Lipschitz for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$, in the full terminal
      payoff vector and hence in $\varphi$ restricted to any subset of the
      coordinates.  (Shift-equivariance in the free coordinates alone is
      false as soon as $\partial A$ contains a terminal of $H$: the payoffs
      of $t_0,t_1$ do not move.)
\item If $H$ is stopping then so is $H_A[\varphi]$ for every $\varphi$, and
      for each positional pair $(\sigma,\tau)$ on $A$ the map
      $\varphi\mapsto v_{\sigma,\tau}(\varphi)$ is \emph{affine}: at $v\in A$
      it equals $\sum_{w\in\partial A}h_{\sigma,\tau}(v,w)\varphi_w$, where
      $h_{\sigma,\tau}(v,w)$ is the probability that the chain started at $v$
      first leaves $A$ at $w$.  Hence
      $R_A=\max_\sigma\min_\tau v_{\sigma,\tau}$ is piecewise affine with at
      most $2^{|C\cap A|}$ distinct affine pieces; the set on which a given
      pair is optimal throughout is a convex polyhedron, cut out by the
      affine local-optimality inequalities, and every linearity domain of
      $R_A$ is a union of such polyhedra (they coincide unless two distinct
      pairs realise the same affine map).
\item The \emph{piece number} $\pi(A):=$ the number of linearity domains of
      $R_A$ is what a dynamic programme over a decomposition must pay: any
      algorithm that stores $R_A$ exactly, as a polyhedral subdivision with
      an affine map on each cell, uses $\Omega(\pi(A))$ space.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(a) Monotonicity is the first line of the proof of \Cref{lem:cut}:
$\varphi\le\varphi'$ gives $T_{H_A[\varphi]}\le T_{H_A[\varphi']}$
pointwise, hence $\lfp\le\lfp$.  For the shift, write $\psi$ for the full
vector of terminal payoffs and $S_c(x):=x+c\mathbf 1$.  At a non-terminal
every operator commutes with $S_c$ ($\max$, $\min$ and the mean do), and at
a terminal the $\psi+c\mathbf 1$ operator returns $\psi_w+c$; so that
operator is $S_c\circ T_\psi\circ S_c^{-1}$ and the least fixed points
correspond.  Monotonicity together with shift-equivariance in $\psi$ gives
$\val(\psi)\le\val(\psi'+\lVert\psi-\psi'\rVert_\infty\mathbf 1)
=\val(\psi')+\lVert\psi-\psi'\rVert_\infty\mathbf 1$ and symmetrically;
applying this to payoff vectors that agree outside a set of coordinates
gives the last clause.

(b) A trap of $H_A[\varphi]$ (\Cref{lem:trapchar}) is a set of
non-terminals of $H_A[\varphi]$, hence a subset of $A$, whose average
vertices have both successors inside and whose controlled vertices have
one; the same holds in $H$, so it is a trap of $H$ and therefore empty.
Stopping makes $I-P_{\sigma,\tau}$ invertible on $A$
(\Cref{lem:denominator}), and $v_{\sigma,\tau}=(I-P)^{-1}r$ with $r$ the
vector of one-step probabilities into $\partial A$ weighted by $\varphi$;
expanding $(I-P)^{-1}=\sum_kP^k$ identifies the coefficient of $\varphi_w$
as the first-passage probability.  \Cref{thm:stopping-determinacy} gives
$\val=\max_\sigma\min_\tau v_{\sigma,\tau}$, a max--min of affine maps; the
region where a fixed pair is optimal is cut out by the affine inequalities
of local optimality (\Cref{lem:local-global}), hence convex, and $R_A$ is
affine on it.  (c) is immediate.
\end{proof}

The tables are exponential, and they are exponential at bounded width.

\begin{theorem}[The tables explode at pathwidth four]\label{tw:fold-width}
Let $P_D$ be the family of \Cref{thm:fold}, with $|V|=6D+2$ and $6D$
non-terminals, and let $A:=V\setminus\{u,t_0,t_1\}$, so that
$\partial A=\{u,t_0,t_1\}$ and $R_A$ is a function of the single free
parameter $\theta=\varphi_u$.  Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item the coordinate of $R_A$ at $F_D$ has exactly $2^{D}=2^{(|V|-2)/6}$
      affine pieces, with breakpoints exactly $j2^{-D}$, $1\le j\le2^{D}-1$,
      and $\pi(A)=2^{D}$ as well --- the optimal pairs on those $2^{D}$
      intervals are pairwise distinct (verified exactly for $D\le8$);
\item $\tw(P_D)=\pw(P_D)=2$ for $D=1$, $=3$ for $D=2,3$, and $=4$ for
      $D=4$; moreover $\pw(P_D)\le4$ for every $D$, by an explicit path
      decomposition, and $\pw(P_D)>3$ for $4\le D\le 8$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently there is no bound of the form $\pi\le\mathrm{poly}(N,\tw)$:
already at treewidth four the exact response tables of a decomposition have
$2^{\Omega(N)}$ pieces, and every dynamic programme that stores them is
exponential.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) is \Cref{thm:fold} together with the slope alternation proved there;
it was re-verified here in exact arithmetic, for $D\le8$, at every dyadic
grid point $j2^{-D}$, every midpoint, and five off-grid rationals, against
backward induction, with the slope set exactly $\{0,2^{-D}\}$ each time.

(ii) The exact values are the elimination-ordering and vertex-separation
dynamic programmes run on $\Gamma(P_D)$, which has $6D$ vertices; they are
feasible for $6D\le18$ and give the stated numbers for $D\le3$.  For the
upper bound take the layout
\[
  u,\;X_1,\;k_{2D-1},\;Y_1,\;F_1,\;G_1,\;
  \bigl(k_{2D-2d+2},\,k_{2D-2d+1},\,X_d,\,Y_d,\,F_d,\,G_d\bigr)_{d=2}^{D},
\]
and the bags $B_i:=\{v_i\}\cup\{u\in S_{i-1}: u$ has a neighbour outside
$S_{i-1}\}$, where $S_{i}$ is the set of the first $i$ vertices.  This is a
path decomposition of $\Gamma(P_D)$ of width $4$; it was verified to be one
for $D\le12$ and for $D=20,30,45,60$.  The lower bound $\pw>3$ for
$4\le D\le8$ is an exhaustive search over the layouts of frontier width at
most $3$, which finds none.  Finally $\tw\le\pw$, and $\tw(P_4)>3$ by the
same exhaustive search for elimination orderings of width $3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{tw:fold-remark}
$P_D$ is acyclic, so backward induction solves it in linear time: the
theorem is a statement about the \emph{tables}, not about the instances.
\Cref{tw:cyclic} closes $P_D$ into a cycle so that the table cannot be
side-stepped, and shows that the \emph{search} of \Cref{tw:tarski} still
finds the fixed point in four queries where the table has $2^{D}$ pieces.
\end{remark}

The explosion needs a two-dimensional interface, and that is sharp.

\begin{proposition}[One live value gives linearly many pieces]\label{tw:one-live}
Let $H$ be a payoff game with no directed cycle among its non-terminals,
let $z$ be a terminal, let $Z$ be the set of non-terminals from which $z$
is reachable, and suppose every vertex of $Z$ has \emph{at most one}
successor in $Z\cup\{z\}$.  Then for every $v$ the map
$\theta\mapsto\val_{H[z:=\theta]}(v)$ is monotone, $1$-Lipschitz and
piecewise affine with at most $|Z|+1$ pieces.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Off $Z$ the value does not depend on $\theta$.  Order $Z$ by a topological
order of the acyclic digraph.  Each $v\in Z$ has exactly one successor
$w\in Z\cup\{z\}$ (at most one by hypothesis, at least one because $z$ is
reachable), and its other successor $w'$ has a $\theta$-independent value
$c_v$.  Hence $f_v(\theta)=\mathrm{op}_v(f_w(\theta),c_v)$ with
$\mathrm{op}_v\in\{\max(\cdot,c),\min(\cdot,c),\tfrac12(\cdot+c)\}$ and
$f_z(\theta)=\theta$.  Each such map is monotone and $1$-Lipschitz, and it
increases the number of affine pieces by at most one (by exactly zero for
the mean).  Induction along the order gives the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{tw:one-live-remark}
Every value of a game is \emph{nondecreasing} in every other value
(\Cref{lem:monotone}), so a one-dimensional interface transports a
composition of monotone one-variable maps, whose preimages of a breakpoint
are single points: no folding is possible and the count is linear.  The
fold of \Cref{thm:fold} is precisely a two-dimensional interface: $F_d$ and
$G_d$ read the \emph{same} pair $(X_d,Y_d)$, and $\max-\min=|{\cdot}|$ in
the difference coordinate, which is not monotone.  This locates the
threshold between \Cref{tw:one-live} and \Cref{tw:fold-width} exactly at
interface dimension two.  Whether the clock track --- the chain
$k_1,\dots,k_{2D-1}$, which supplies the shrinking constants $4^{-d}$ and
is the third live value --- can be dispensed with, i.e.\ whether some
stopping family of pathwidth $2$ or $3$ has a response function with
$2^{\Omega(N)}$ pieces, is left open; see the GAP at the end of this
section.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[A fold needs a constant]\label{tw:no-clock}
Let $\Lambda$ be a gadget with two \emph{input} vertices, carrying values
$f,g$ supplied from outside, and two \emph{output} vertices, every internal
vertex of which has both successors among the internal and input vertices
--- so $\Lambda$ reads no terminal --- and from every internal vertex of
which an input is reachable, so that $\Lambda$ with its inputs read as
terminals is a stopping payoff game.  Let $\Phi(f,g)\in\mathbb R^{2}$ be the
pair of output values.  Then
\[
  \Phi(f+c,g+c)=\Phi(f,g)+c\mathbf 1,\qquad \Phi(\lambda f,\lambda g)=\lambda\Phi(f,g)
  \quad(\lambda>0),
\]
so $\Phi_1-\Phi_2=\psi(f-g)$ with $\psi(d)=\alpha d$ for $d\ge0$ and
$\psi(d)=\beta|d|$ for $d\le0$; $\psi^{D}$ has at most two affine pieces for
every $D$; and in a chain of $D$ copies of $\Lambda$ the linearity domains
of the composed map, as a function of the initial difference $f_0-g_0$, are
at most two.  A fold that accumulates therefore requires the gadget to read
a terminal.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\max$, $\min$ and the mean all commute with $x\mapsto x+c$ and with
$x\mapsto\lambda x$ applied to both arguments, and every internal value is
obtained from $f,g$ by those three operations; formally, the shifted
operator is $S_c\circ T\circ S_c^{-1}$ and the scaled one is
$M_\lambda\circ T\circ M_\lambda^{-1}$, and $\Lambda$ being stopping its
fixed point is unique (\Cref{thm:contraction}), so the fixed points
correspond.  (The stopping hypothesis is needed: a gadget containing an
internal cycle from which no input is reachable has value $0$ there by
least-fixed-point semantics, and that value does not move when the inputs
do.)  Additive
homogeneity gives $\Phi_i(f,g)=g+\Phi_i(f-g,0)$, so
$\Phi_1-\Phi_2=\psi(f-g)$ with $\psi(d):=\Phi_1(d,0)-\Phi_2(d,0)$, and
positive homogeneity gives $\psi(\lambda d)=\lambda\psi(d)$, i.e.\ the two
half-lines are scaled by $\alpha:=\psi(1)$ and $\beta:=\psi(-1)$.  A
composition of maps that are linear on each of $[0,\infty)$ and
$(-\infty,0]$ and send $0$ to $0$ is again of that form, so $\psi^{D}$ has
at most two pieces, and $\mathrm{sign}(\psi^{j}(d_0))$ is determined by
$\mathrm{sign}(d_0)$ for every $j$; since the whole orbit of $\Phi$ is
determined by $d_0$, $g_0$ and those signs, the linearity domains in $d_0$
are at most two.  (Verified on $3000$ random terminal-free gadgets in exact
arithmetic --- all of them acyclic, hence stopping --- no violation of
either identity, and the difference map $\psi$ of $400$ of them has at most
two affine pieces, breaking only at $0$.)
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The shape of GAP 2]\label{tw:gap2-shape}
\Cref{tw:no-clock} says the fold of \Cref{thm:fold} cannot be run by a
chain of identical terminal-free gadgets.  A gadget may read $t_0$ without
costing any width, since terminals are not vertices of $\Gamma$; then
$\Phi$ is still positively homogeneous but no longer additively so, the
state reduces to the projective coordinate $r=g/f$, and the level map
becomes a piecewise-M\"obius map $\psi(r)=\Phi_2(1,r)/\Phi_1(1,r)$ with
$\Phi_1,\Phi_2$ monotone, $1$-Lipschitz and nondecreasing in $r$.  GAP 2 is
therefore, for chains of a fixed gadget, exactly this: \emph{is there such a
$\psi$ with a nondegenerate invariant interval $J$ on which $\psi$ has two
monotone branches, each mapping $J$ onto $J$?}  If not, the constants have
to shrink with the level, they have to come from a track of their own, and
that track is the third live value that makes $\pw(P_D)=4$.

Two searches say ``probably not'', and neither is a proof.  (a) Taking the
closure of $\{0,\,f,\,g\}$ under $\max$, $\min$ and the mean for three
rounds, capped at $260$ piecewise-linear functions of
$r\in[0,1]$ (writing $f=1-r$, $g=r$), and forming $\psi=B/(A+B)$ for all
$59\,315$ admissible ordered pairs $(A,B)$ from that closure, the largest
piece count of $\psi^{D}$ over $D=1,\dots,9$ that occurs anywhere is
$5,13,23,35,49,65,83,101,119$ --- quadratic in $D$, against $2^{D}=512$ at
$D=9$.  (b) Allowing the gadget to read $t_1$ as well, so that
$\Phi:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1]^{2}$ is a general autonomous monotone nonexpansive
piecewise-affine map, the number of distinct itineraries of $\Phi^{D}$ on an
exact $25\times25$ rational grid saturates at $11$ within three steps, over
$200$ random gadgets of depth up to $7$.  Search (a) is exhaustive over a
finite closure and search (b) is random, which by the standing experience of
this project is no evidence at all; both are reported as measurements.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The piece-bounded dynamic programme, and why we do not keep it]\label{tw:dp-remark}
The dynamic programme this section started from stores, at every node $t$ of
a tree decomposition, the response function $R_{A_t}$ of the part $A_t$
below $t$ as a polyhedral subdivision of $[0,1]^{\partial A_t}$ with an
affine map on each cell, and glues two children by composing the tables and
taking the fixed point of the composition, which is legitimate by
\Cref{lem:cut,tw:cut-sign}.  For fixed width $k$ it runs in time polynomial
in $n$ and in $\pi(G):=\max_t\pi(A_t)$, so \emph{``treewidth $k$ and piece
number $\pi$ polynomial''} is a polynomial class.  We name it and drop it,
for three reasons.  (i) $\pi$ is not known to be checkable in polynomial
time: it counts the regions on which one optimal pair is optimal, and
deciding that one such region is nonempty is a feasibility question about
the very game one is solving.  (ii) By \Cref{tw:fold-width} it is
$2^{\Omega(N)}$ already at treewidth four, and by \Cref{tw:cyclic} the same
table sits inside a genuine cycle, where it cannot be side-stepped by
choosing the sweep direction.  (iii) \Cref{tw:qp} attains
$n^{O(k\log n)}$ with \emph{no} hypothesis on $\pi$, so on every family
where the table programme is polynomial the search is at worst
quasipolynomial, while on $P_D^{\circ}$ the search is polynomial and the
table programme is not.  The piece number is the right parameter to name
and the wrong parameter to keep.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Freezing, and the sign of the residual}

\Cref{lem:cut} already provides the object a decomposition needs.  On
stopping games it has a two-sided sign property that the search below uses,
and which the proof of \Cref{lem:cut} contains but does not state.

\begin{lemma}[The cut map is sign-definite]\label{tw:cut-sign}
Let $H$ be a \emph{stopping} payoff game, $S$ a set of non-terminals, and
$F_S$ the cut map of \Cref{lem:cut}.  Then $H[x]$ is stopping for every
$x\in[0,1]^{S}$, $F_S$ is monotone, $\val_H|_S$ is its \emph{unique} fixed
point, and for every $x\in[0,1]^{S}$
\[
  F_S(x)\le x\ \Longrightarrow\ x\ge\val_H|_S,
  \qquad
  F_S(x)\ge x\ \Longrightarrow\ x\le\val_H|_S .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Stopping: a trap of $H[x]$ avoids the terminals, hence avoids $S$, and is
then a trap of $H$, hence empty (\Cref{lem:trapchar}).  Monotonicity and
$\val_H|_S=\lfp(F_S)$ are \Cref{lem:cut}.  Let $\hat x$ be $x$ on $S$ and
$\val_{H[x]}$ off $S$.  By \eqref{eq:assembly}, $F_S(x)\le x$ gives
$T_H\hat x\le\hat x$ and $F_S(x)\ge x$ gives $T_H\hat x\ge\hat x$; since
$H$ is stopping, \Cref{cor:comparison} turns these into
$\val_H\le\hat x$ and $\val_H\ge\hat x$ respectively, and restricting to
$S$ gives the two implications.  Applying both to a fixed point gives
uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Divide-and-conquer search for the cut fixed point]\label{tw:tarski}
Let $L$ be a finite chain with $M$ elements, identified with
$\{0,\dots,M-1\}$, and let $F:L^{d}\to L^{d}$ be monotone.  Then a fixed point of $F$ is found with at most
$2(\lceil\log_2M\rceil+1)^{d}$ evaluations of $F$, by the following
recursion on $d$.  On a box $[\mathrm{lo},\mathrm{hi}]$ into which $F$ maps
itself: if $d=0$ return the empty tuple; otherwise put $m$ the midpoint of
the $d$-th coordinate range, find recursively a fixed point $y^\ast$ of the
$(d-1)$-dimensional slice map $g(y):=\bigl(F(y,m)\bigr)_{<d}$, put
$x:=(y^\ast,m)$ and evaluate $F(x)$; if $F(x)_d=m$ return $x$; if
$F(x)_d>m$ recurse on $[F(x),\mathrm{hi}]$; if $F(x)_d<m$ recurse on
$[\mathrm{lo},F(x)]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Invariant.}  $F$ maps $[\mathrm{lo},\mathrm{hi}]$ into itself, so by
Knaster--Tarski the box contains a fixed point.  The slice map $g$ maps
$[\mathrm{lo}_{<d},\mathrm{hi}_{<d}]$ into itself and is monotone, so the
recursive call is legitimate; and $F(x)_{<d}=g(y^\ast)=y^\ast=x_{<d}$.  If
$F(x)_d>m$ then $F(x)\ge x$, so for $y\ge F(x)$ one has
$F(y)\ge F(F(x))\ge F(x)$ (monotonicity applied to $F(x)\ge x$) and
$F(y)\le F(\mathrm{hi})\le\mathrm{hi}$: the invariant holds on
$[F(x),\mathrm{hi}]$.  The case $F(x)_d<m$ is symmetric.

\emph{Progress.}  In the first case the new lower corner has $d$-th
coordinate $F(x)_d\ge m+1$, in the second the new upper corner has $d$-th
coordinate $\le m-1$; either way the $d$-th coordinate range at least
halves.  If that range is a single point then, $F$ mapping the box into
itself, $F(x)_d=m$ and the loop returns.

\emph{Cost.}  Write $Q(d,M)$ for the number of evaluations.  Each outer
iteration costs one evaluation plus one recursive call, and there are at
most $\lceil\log_2M\rceil+1$ iterations, so
$Q(d,M)\le(\lceil\log_2M\rceil+1)(Q(d-1,M)+1)$ with $Q(0,M)=0$, whence
$Q(d,M)\le2(\lceil\log_2M\rceil+1)^{d}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{tw:tarski-prior}
The scheme is the divide-and-conquer of Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein
and Yannakakis for the \textsc{Tarski} fixed-point problem, and the
$O(\log^{d}M)$ query bound is theirs; Fearnley, P\'alv\"olgyi and Savani
improve the exponent, and Chen and Li prove lower bounds (all from memory,
unchecked against the sources).  The cut above uses $F(x)$ rather than $x$
as the new corner, which makes the progress argument elementary and removes
the need for the recursive call to return a \emph{least} fixed point.  What
is new here is not the search but its coupling with \Cref{lem:cut}: the
game supplies a monotone map whose fixed point is unique and sign-definite,
on a lattice of size $2^{O(N)}$, in dimension equal to the size of the
frozen set.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Rounding the cut map onto a grid]\label{tw:round}
Let $H$ be stopping, $S$ a set of non-terminals, $L\subseteq[0,1]$ a finite
chain containing $0$ and $1$ whose consecutive elements differ by at most
$\varepsilon$, and $\lceil\cdot\rceil_L$ the round-up to $L$.  Then
$F^{L}:=\lceil\cdot\rceil_L\circ F_S$ maps $L^{S}$ into $L^{S}$
monotonically, and every fixed point $\hat\theta$ of $F^{L}$ satisfies
\[
  \val_H|_S\;\le\;\hat\theta\;\le\;\val_H|_S+N2^{a}\varepsilon\,\mathbf 1 ,
\]
where $N$ is the total number of vertices of $H$, terminals included.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Monotone: a round-up to a chain is monotone.  $\hat\theta\ge F_S(\hat\theta)$
gives $\hat\theta\ge\val_H|_S$ by \Cref{tw:cut-sign}.  Also
$\hat\theta\le F_S(\hat\theta)+\varepsilon\mathbf 1$; with
$\hat x$ the assembly of $\hat\theta$ as in \eqref{eq:assembly} this reads
$T_H\hat x\le\hat x\le T_H\hat x+\varepsilon\mathbf 1$.  By
\Cref{thm:contraction} --- whose proof compares two finite-horizon games
that differ only in the terminal payoff function, so it holds verbatim for
payoff games (\Cref{lem:gen-comparison}) ---
$\lVert T^{k}\hat x-T^{k+1}\hat x\rVert_\infty\le
(1-2^{-a})^{\lfloor k/N\rfloor}\lVert\hat x-T\hat x\rVert_\infty$, so
$\lVert\hat x-\val_H\rVert_\infty\le\sum_{k\ge0}\lVert T^{k}\hat x-T^{k+1}\hat x\rVert_\infty
\le N2^{a}\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact recovery]\label{tw:recover}
Let $H$ be stopping and let $\Delta$ be a common denominator of its
terminal payoffs.  Then every coordinate of $\val_H$ is a rational whose
denominator divides a positive integer at most $Q:=\Delta2^{a}$.  If
$\lvert\hat\theta_v-\val_H(v)\rvert<1/(2Q^{2})$ then $\val_H(v)$ is the
unique rational with denominator at most $Q$ in that interval, and the
continued-fraction expansion of $\hat\theta_v$ returns it in
$O(\log Q)$ arithmetic steps.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a positional pair, $v_{\sigma,\tau}=A_U^{-1}b$ with $A_U$ as in
\Cref{lem:denominator} and $b$ a vector of $\tfrac12$-combinations of the
payoffs, so $\Delta b$ is integral; Cramer's rule and
$\det A_U\le2^{a}$ (\Cref{lem:denominator-sharp}) give the denominator
bound, and $\val_H=v_{\sigma^\ast,\tau^\ast}$ for the optimal pair.  Two
distinct rationals with denominators at most $Q$ differ by at least
$1/Q^{2}$, which gives uniqueness; and a rational $p/q$ with $q\le Q$ and
$|x-p/q|<1/(2q^{2})$ is a convergent of $x$ (Legendre), so it is found
among the $O(\log Q)$ convergents.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A polynomial class: modulators}

\begin{definition}[Freezing-closed class, modulator]\label{tw:modulator-def}
A class $\mathcal P$ of payoff games is \emph{freezing-closed} if
$H\in\mathcal P$ implies $H[x]\in\mathcal P$ for every set of non-terminals
retyped as terminals with arbitrary payoffs.  For a payoff game $H$ put
\[
  \mu_{\mathcal P}(H)\;:=\;\min\{|X| : X\subseteq V\setminus\text{terminals},\;
  H[X{:=}\theta]\in\mathcal P\ \text{for every }\theta\},
\]
the \emph{$\mathcal P$-modulator number}.  Writing $\mathcal A_k$ for the
$k$-acyclic games ($k\in\{\max,\min,\mathrm{avg}\}$) we abbreviate
$\mu_k:=\mu_{\mathcal A_k}$; since freezing a vertex deletes its out-edges,
$\mu_k(H)$ is the least number of vertices meeting every directed cycle
through a kind-$k$ vertex.  The classes
$\mathcal A_{\max},\mathcal A_{\min},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{avg}}$
(\Cref{thm:kacyclic}), the acyclic games, the games with $a\le a_0$
(\Cref{thm:few-avg}), the games in $\mathcal K_k$
(\Cref{thm:bounded-components}) and the games carrying an escape
certificate of a fixed rate (\Cref{thm:escape-class}) are all
freezing-closed: freezing deletes edges, so it destroys cycles, cannot
raise $a$, cannot add an edge of $H(G)$, and only lowers the survival
operator (a new terminal is read as $0$).  \Cref{thm:few-denominator} is
\emph{not} freezing-closed in any useful sense, since a frozen grid value
carries a large denominator of its own.  To be usable in
\Cref{tw:modulator} a class must moreover come with a solver for
\emph{payoff} games, that is for arbitrary terminal payoffs;
\Cref{thm:kacyclic} is stated in exactly that generality, which is why
$\mathcal A_{\max},\mathcal A_{\min},\mathcal A_{\mathrm{avg}}$ are the
instances of \Cref{tw:modulator} we use.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The modulator class]\label{tw:modulator}
Let $\mathcal P$ be freezing-closed and solvable exactly in time
$p(n,\beta)$ on games with $n$ non-terminals and payoffs of bit-size
$\beta$.  Let $G$ be a stopping payoff game with $\mu:=\mu_{\mathcal P}(G)$
and let $X$ attain it.  Then $\val_G$ is computed exactly in time
\[
  O\!\left(\,(B+2)^{\mu}\cdot p\bigl(n,O(B)\bigr)\;+\;\mathrm{poly}(n,B)\right),
  \qquad B=O\bigl(a+\log N+\log\Delta\bigr),
\]
where $\Delta$ is a common denominator of the payoffs of $G$; for an SSG,
$B=O(a+\log N)=O(N)$ and the bound is $N^{O(\mu)}p(N,O(N))$.  In
particular \Cref{prob:main} is decidable in polynomial time on every family
with $\mu_{\mathcal P}=O(1)$, and in time $N^{O(\mu)}$ in general.  The
algorithm is self-certifying: it ends by verifying $T_Gw=w$ exactly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $Q:=\Delta2^{a}$, $\varepsilon:=1/(4N2^{a}Q^{2})$ and let $L$ be the
dyadic grid of mesh $2^{-B}\le\varepsilon$, $B=\lceil\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil$;
$B=O(a+\log N+\log\Delta)$ because $\log Q=\log\Delta+a$.  The cut map
$F_X$ of \Cref{lem:cut} is evaluated at a grid point $\theta$ by solving
$G[X{:=}\theta]\in\mathcal P$ exactly --- one call to the $\mathcal P$-solver,
on payoffs of bit-size $O(B+\log\Delta)$ --- and then applying
$\mathrm{op}_x$ at each $x\in X$; this is exact, so the computed map is
exactly $F_X$ and hence monotone.  By \Cref{tw:round}, $F^{L}$ is a
monotone self-map of the finite lattice $L^{X}$, so \Cref{tw:tarski}
returns a fixed point $\hat\theta$ with at most $2(B+2)^{\mu}$ evaluations,
and $0\le\hat\theta-\val_G|_X\le N2^{a}\varepsilon\mathbf 1<1/(2Q^{2})$.
\Cref{tw:recover} recovers $\val_G|_X$ exactly by continued fractions.  One
further $\mathcal P$-solve at $\theta=\val_G|_X$ gives the values off $X$
(\Cref{lem:cut}, last clause), and $T_Gw=w$ is checked exactly; a stopping
game has a unique fixed point (\Cref{thm:contraction}), so the check
certifies the output.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The question of \Cref{rem:kacyclic}]\label{tw:kacyclic-mu}
For $k\in\{\max,\min,\mathrm{avg}\}$ and $\mu_k$ as above, the value vector
of a stopping SSG is computable exactly in time $N^{O(\mu_k)}$, and in
polynomial time whenever $\mu_k=O(1)$.  For $\mu_k=0$ this is
\Cref{thm:kacyclic}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Prior art]\label{tw:modulator-prior}
With $\mathcal P$ the acyclic games, $\mu_{\mathcal P}$ is exactly the
feedback vertex number, and \Cref{tw:modulator} then says that
\textsc{SSG-Value} is decidable in time $N^{O(\mathrm{fvs})}$.  That a
bounded feedback vertex number makes simple stochastic games polynomial is
Auger--Coucheney--Strozecki's work on almost-acyclic simple stochastic
games, already listed among the prior art this project has rediscovered
(from memory, unchecked against the source; whether their bound is
$\mathrm{FPT}$ or $\mathrm{XP}$ in that parameter, and what exactly their
parameter is, cannot be checked here).  The proof above is different --- a
Tarski search rather than a dichotomy on the values --- and, more to the
point, the parameter is not the feedback vertex number but the
$\mathcal P$-modulator number, which can be $1$ where the feedback vertex
number is $\Theta(N)$ (\Cref{tw:family}).  For $\mathcal P=\mathcal A_k$ the
statement answers the question \Cref{rem:kacyclic} leaves open, namely
what happens when $\mu_k>0$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[One-coloured feedback]\label{tw:colour-feedback}
For $k\in\{\max,\min\}$ let $f_k(G)$ be the number of kind-$k$ vertices
lying on a directed cycle of $G$.  Then the value vector of an arbitrary
SSG --- stopping or not --- is computable exactly in time
$\mathrm{poly}(N)\,2^{f_k(G)}$, hence in polynomial time when
$f_k=O(\log N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $F$ be the set of kind-$k$ vertices on cycles, $k=\max$ say.  For each
of the $2^{|F|}$ maps $\rho:F\to V$ with $\rho(v)\in\{v^{(0)},v^{(1)}\}$
let $G_\rho$ be $G$ with every $v\in F$ retyped as an \emph{average} vertex
with both out-edges to $\rho(v)$; the operator at $v$ then returns the
value of $\rho(v)$, exactly as it would if Max were frozen to $\rho$ there,
so $\val_{G_\rho}$ is the value of the game in which Max is frozen to
$\rho$ on $F$ and free elsewhere.  No Max vertex of $G_\rho$ lies on a cycle --- those
of $F$ are no longer Max, and those outside $F$ lie on no cycle by the
choice of $F$ --- so $G_\rho$ is $\max$-acyclic and \Cref{thm:kacyclic}
computes $\val_{G_\rho}$ exactly in polynomial time, with no stopping
hypothesis.  By positional determinacy (\Cref{thm:determinacy}) an optimal
$\sigma^\ast$ exists; $\val_{G_\rho}\le\val$ for every $\rho$ because Max
is restricted, with equality at $\rho=\sigma^\ast|_F$.  So
$\val=\max_\rho\val_{G_\rho}$.  For $k=\min$ replace $\max$ by $\min$ and
$\max$-acyclic by $\min$-acyclic.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{tw:colour-vs-modulator}
$\mu_k\le f_k$ always, since the kind-$k$ vertices on cycles meet every
cycle through a kind-$k$ vertex; so \Cref{tw:modulator} applies whenever
\Cref{tw:colour-feedback} does, with the better bound $N^{O(\mu_k)}$ when
$\mu_k$ is bounded and the worse one $N^{O(f_k)}$ against $2^{f_k}$ when
$f_k$ is logarithmic.  The two are therefore incomparable and both are
worth having.  Neither is available for $k=\mathrm{avg}$: a coin cannot be
frozen.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Bounded treewidth}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded treewidth is quasipolynomial]\label{tw:qp}
Let $G$ be a stopping payoff game with $n$ non-terminals, terminal payoffs
of common denominator $\Delta$, and a tree decomposition of $\Gamma(G)$ of
width $k$ (given; one is computed in linear time for fixed $k$ by
Bodlaender's algorithm, from memory, unchecked).  Then $\val_G$ is computed exactly with
$2^{O(k\log^{2}n)}=n^{O(k\log n)}$ arithmetic operations on rationals of
$O\bigl(n^{1+\log_23}+n^{\log_23}\log\Delta\bigr)$ bits.
In particular \textsc{SSG-Value} restricted to any family of treewidth
$O(1)$ is decidable in quasipolynomial time $N^{O(\log N)}$, and the
algorithm certifies its own output by checking $Tw=w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The recursion.}  If $G$ has no directed cycle among its
non-terminals, backward induction returns $\val_G$ in linear time.  If
$n\le2(k+1)$, brute force over the $2^{|C|}\le2^{2(k+1)}$ positional pairs
returns it (\Cref{thm:stopping-determinacy}).  If $\Gamma(G)$ is
disconnected, each component is successor-closed up to terminals and is
solved separately (\Cref{lem:successor-closed}), so assume it connected.
Otherwise the standard
centroid argument gives a bag $X$ of the decomposition, $|X|\le k+1$, such
that every connected component of $\Gamma(G)-X$ has at most $n/2$ vertices:
orient every edge of the decomposition tree towards the side carrying more
than $n/2$ vertices, take a node all of whose incident edges point to it,
and note that every component of $\Gamma(G)-X$ lies entirely on the far
side of one incident edge.  The bag $X$ is nonempty, since otherwise
$\Gamma(G)$ would itself be a component of $n>n/2$ vertices.  Let
$C_1,\dots,C_r$ be those components.  Because $C_i$ is a
component of $\Gamma(G)-X$, every successor of a vertex of $C_i$ lies in
$C_i\cup X\cup\{\text{terminals}\}$; so for $\theta\in[0,1]^{X}$ the game
$G_i[\theta]$ on $C_i$, with $X$ retyped as terminals of payoff $\theta$,
is well defined, is stopping (\Cref{tw:cut-sign}), has at most $n/2$
non-terminals, and inherits the tree decomposition of width $\le k$
obtained by intersecting every bag with $C_i$.  Solving all the
$G_i[\theta]$ recursively and applying $\mathrm{op}_x$ at each $x\in X$
evaluates the cut map $F_X$ of \Cref{lem:cut} exactly at $\theta$.

\emph{The search at one node.}  Exactly as in the proof of
\Cref{tw:modulator}: with $Q=\Delta2^{a}$, $\varepsilon=1/(4N2^{a}Q^{2})$
and $L$ the dyadic grid of mesh $2^{-B}$, $B=\lceil\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil
\le 3a+2\log_2\Delta+\log_2 n+3$, the rounded map $F^{L}$ is a monotone
self-map of $L^{X}$ (\Cref{tw:round}), \Cref{tw:tarski} finds a fixed point
in at most $2(B+2)^{k+1}$ evaluations, \Cref{tw:round} bounds the error by
$N2^{a}\varepsilon<1/(2Q^{2})$ and \Cref{tw:recover} recovers
$\val_G|_X$ exactly.  One more round of recursive solves at
$\theta=\val_G|_X$ gives the values off $X$, and $T_Gw=w$ certifies.

\emph{Bit-size.}  Write $\delta_j$ for $\log_2$ of the common denominator
of the payoffs at recursion depth $j$, so $\delta_0=\log_2\Delta$.  The
children of a node at depth $j$ receive payoffs from the grid $L$ together
with the payoffs of the node, so
$\delta_{j+1}\le\delta_j+B\le3\delta_j+3a+\log_2n+3\le3\delta_j+4n$ (using $a\le n$).
The depth is at most $\log_2n$, so
$\delta_j\le3^{\log_2n}\bigl(\delta_0+2n\bigr)=O\bigl(n^{\log_23}(n+\delta_0)\bigr)$,
and every number handled has $O(n^{1+\log_23}+n^{\log_23}\delta_0)$ bits;
in particular $B=O(n^{1+\log_23}+n^{\log_23}\delta_0)$ throughout.

\emph{Cost.}  Let $T(n)$ be the time on $n$ non-terminals.  At one node the
number of recursive solves is at most $2(B+2)^{k+1}+1=n^{O(k)}$ (for an SSG,
$\delta_0=0$ and $B=O(n^{2.585})$, so $(B+2)^{k+1}=n^{O(k)}$), each on a set
of components of total size at most $n$ with every component of size at most
$n/2$.  If $T(m)/m$ is nondecreasing then
$\sum_iT(n_i)\le\bigl(\sum_in_i\bigr)T(n/2)/(n/2)\le2T(n/2)$, so
$T(n)\le n^{O(k)}\cdot2T(n/2)+\mathrm{poly}$, whence
$T(n)\le\bigl(2n^{O(k)}\bigr)^{\log_2n}\mathrm{poly}=2^{O(k\log^{2}n)}\mathrm{poly}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What \Cref{tw:qp} does and does not settle]\label{tw:qp-remark}
Two readings should be resisted.  First, the bound is quasipolynomial, not
polynomial, and it is quasipolynomial for a structural reason: the balanced
separator recursion re-solves both sides from scratch at every query, so the
query cost is raised to the depth.  Second, the hard families of this
document all have width at most four and are therefore covered ---
$L_n,H_m,G_m,\mathrm{WD},\mathrm{CC}$ are decided in time
$N^{O(\log N)}$ by \Cref{tw:qp}, and all of them by
\Cref{tw:modulator} in polynomial time --- but they were never hard to
\emph{solve}; they are hard for particular \emph{mechanisms}
(\Cref{sec:gap}), and a width bound says nothing about that.  What
\Cref{tw:qp} does buy is a genuine comparison: on games of constant
treewidth it beats \Cref{thm:subexp}'s $e^{2\sqrt n}\mathrm{poly}(N)$ and
\Cref{thm:few-avg}'s $\mathrm{poly}(N)2^{a}$, neither of which is
subexponential there.  It also says where a superpolynomial family for a
mechanism must live if it is to be a genuinely hard \emph{instance}: not at
bounded treewidth, unless quasipolynomial is the truth.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[The search beats the table on the same instance]\label{tw:cyclic}
Let $P_D^{\circ}$ be $P_D$ with $u$ retyped as an average vertex
$u\to(F_D,t_1)$.  Then $P_D^{\circ}$ is a stopping SSG on $6D+2$ vertices
with $\pw\le5$ (and $\tw=\pw=4$ at $D=3$), every cycle of which meets $u$,
so $\mu_{\mathcal P}(P_D^{\circ})=1$ for $\mathcal P$ the acyclic games; its
value is
\[
  \val(u)=\tfrac12+3\cdot2^{-(D+3)}\qquad(D\ge2),
\]
which lies in the middle piece --- the $2^{D-1}$-st of $2^{D}$ --- of the
response function $R_{V\setminus\{u\}}$ of \Cref{tw:fold-width}.  The
algorithm of \Cref{tw:modulator} with $X=\{u\}$ returns the exact value
vector after \emph{four} evaluations of the cut map for every
$2\le D\le12$ (ten at $D=1$), while the exact table has $2^{D}$ pieces.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Stopping, the width bounds and the values are exact computations, carried
out for $D\le12$; the explicit path decomposition of \Cref{tw:fold-width}
with $u$ added to every bag has width $5$, and the exact pathwidth and
treewidth dynamic programmes give $4$ at $D=3$.  Every cycle meets $u$
because $P_D$ itself is acyclic.  The query count is the run of the
implementation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A family inside the modulator class and outside all six}

\begin{definition}[The family $M_n$]\label{tw:family-def}
For $n\ge3$ let $M_n$ be the SSG with non-sink vertices
$h,x_1,\dots,x_n\in\Vmax$, $y_1,\dots,y_n\in\Vmin$,
$b_1,\dots,b_n,c_1,\dots,c_{2n}\in\Vavg$, start vertex $h$, and edges
\[
\begin{gathered}
  h\to(x_1,c_{2n}),\qquad x_i\to(b_i,c_{n+i}),\qquad b_i\to(y_i,c_1),\qquad
  y_i\to(x_{i+1},b_i)\quad(x_{n+1}:=h),\\
  c_j\to(o_j,c_{j+1})\ (j<2n),\qquad c_{2n}\to(t_0,t_1),\qquad
  o_j=\begin{cases}c_1,&j<n\\ t_1,&j=n\\ t_0,&n<j<2n.\end{cases}
\end{gathered}
\]
So $N=5n+3$, $a=3n$, $|\Vmax|=n+1$, $|\Vmin|=n$, and the $c$-part is
exactly $G_n$ of \Cref{thm:vi-lower}.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[$M_n$ is in the modulator class and in none of the six]\label{tw:family}
$M_n$ is stopping, every vertex is reachable from $h$, and:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $\mu_{\max}(M_n)=1$, attained by $X=\{h\}$: $M_n$ is not
      $\max$-acyclic by (iv), and freezing $h$ leaves a
      $\max$-acyclic game, so \Cref{tw:modulator} with $\mathcal P=\mathcal
      A_{\max}$ solves $M_n$ in polynomial time.  The implementation needs
      $10$ or $11$ evaluations of the cut map for every $2\le n\le12$ and
      returns the exact value vector, certified by $Tw=w$;
      $\val(h)=\tfrac12+2^{-(n+1)}$.  (The implementation's residual solver
      is the exact Hoffman--Karp solver rather than the back-substitution of
      \Cref{thm:kacyclic}; that the residual game is $\max$-acyclic, so that
      \Cref{thm:kacyclic} applies and the residual solve is polynomial, is
      checked separately by exhaustive search for a Max-cycle hitting set.)
\item The feedback vertex number of $M_n$ is at least $n+1$: the $n$
      two-cycles $y_i\to b_i\to y_i$ and the two-cycle $c_1\to c_2\to c_1$
      are $n+1$ pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles.  So the modulator number is
      $1$ where the feedback vertex number is $\Theta(N)$.
\item $a=3(N-3)/5$, so \Cref{thm:few-avg} gives only $2^{\Omega(N)}$.
\item The cycle $h\to x_1\to b_1\to y_1\to x_2\to\dots\to y_n\to h$ carries
      a Max, a Min and an average vertex, so $M_n$ is neither $\max$- nor
      $\min$- nor $\mathrm{avg}$-acyclic and \Cref{thm:kacyclic} does not
      apply.
\item $H(M_n)$ is a single strongly connected component on all $n+1$ Max
      vertices, so $M_n\notin\mathcal K_k$ for any $k<n+1$ and
      \Cref{thm:bounded-components} gives only $2^{\Omega(N)}$.
\item $\val(c_1)=\tfrac12+2^{-(n+1)}$ and $\min_j\val(c_j)=2^{-n}$, so the
      common denominator of the value vector is at least $2^{n+1}$ and
      \Cref{thm:few-denominator} gives only $2^{\Omega(N)}$; the value
      alphabet has $n+3$ letters.
\item $d(M_n)\ge n$, so \Cref{thm:few-escape} gives only $2^{\Omega(N)}$.
\item Every escape certificate $(\lambda,x)$ of \Cref{def:survival} for
      $M_n$ has $1-\lambda<4\cdot2^{-n}$, so
      $\log(1/\lambda)<2^{-n+3}$ and \Cref{thm:escape-class} gives at least
      $2^{\Omega(N)}$ rounds.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Stopping.}  Let $U$ be a trap.  It omits $c_{2n}$, whose successors
are the two sinks; then it omits $c_{2n-1},\dots,c_1$ in turn, each being
an average vertex one of whose successors is a sink or an already omitted
$c$; then it omits every $b_i$, an average vertex needing $c_1$; then every
$x_i$, whose successors $b_i,c_{n+i}$ are both out; then every $y_i$, whose
successors $x_{i+1}$ and $b_i$ are both out; then $h$.  So $U=\emptyset$
and \Cref{lem:trapchar} applies.  Reachability is immediate.

(i) The Max vertices are $h$ and $x_1,\dots,x_n$.  Every cycle through an
$x_i$ must return to it, and the only edges out of the block
$\{x_i,b_i,y_i\}$ are $x_i\to c_{n+i}$, $b_i\to c_1$ and $y_i\to x_{i+1}$
(with $x_{n+1}=h$); the $c$-part never leaves itself, so a cycle through
$x_i$ must run forward through $x_{i+1},\dots,x_n,h$ and back, hence meet
$h$.  Freezing $h$ therefore destroys every cycle through a Max vertex, and
$M_n[h{:=}\theta]$ is $\max$-acyclic.  It is not acyclic: the two-cycles
$y_i\leftrightarrow b_i$ and the cycles inside the $c$-part survive.  The
value and query counts are the run of the implementation, certified by
$T w=w$ and cross-checked against brute-force $\max$--$\min$ for
$n\le4$.

(ii) The listed cycles are vertex-disjoint: $\{y_i,b_i\}$ for $i=1,\dots,n$
and $\{c_1,c_2\}$ (using $c_1\to c_2\to c_1$, valid because $o_2=c_1$ for
$n>2$).

(iii)--(v) are read off the definition; for (v), $H(M_n)$ contains
$h\to x_1\to\dots\to x_n\to h$ along the ring, so all $n+1$ Max vertices
are in one component (\Cref{def:maxreach}).

(vi) The set $\{c_1,\dots,c_{2n},t_0,t_1\}$ is closed under successors, so
by \Cref{lem:successor-closed} the values there are those of $G_n$, and
\Cref{thm:vi-lower} gives $\val(c_1)=\tfrac12+2^{-(n+1)}$ and
$\min_j\val(c_j)=2^{-n}$.  The alphabet count and the exact common
denominator $2^{n+1}$ are exact computations for $n\le12$.

(vii) In \Cref{lem:descent}'s filtration, $c_n\in C_1$ (its successor $t_1$
is in $C_0$), and inductively $c_{n-i}\in C_{i+1}$, so
$\ell(c_i)=n-i+1$ for $1\le i\le n$, while $\ell(c_{n+1})=n$.  For
$i<n$ the successors of $c_i$ are $c_1$, of level $n\ge\ell(c_i)$, and
$c_{i+1}$, of level $\ell(c_i)-1$: exactly one of strictly smaller level,
so $\omega(c_i)=1$; and $c_n$ has successors $t_1$ (level $0$) and
$c_{n+1}$ (level $n>1$), so $\omega(c_n)=1$.  The descent path
$c_1\to c_2\to\dots\to c_n\to t_1$ therefore has
$\sum_i\omega(p_i)=n$, so $A_\sigma(c_1)\ge n$ for every $\sigma$, and
$c_1\in C_\infty$ because $\val(c_1)>0$; hence $d(\sigma)\ge n$ for every
optimal $\sigma$ and $d(M_n)\ge n$.  (The implementation finds
$d(M_n)=n+1$, the optimal Max strategy being unique for $n\le7$.)

(viii) Let $x\ge\mathbf 1$ satisfy $Sx\le\lambda x$.  For $1\le i<n$ the
vertex $c_i$ is average with successors $c_1$ and $c_{i+1}$, so
$\tfrac12(x(c_1)+x(c_{i+1}))\le\lambda x(c_i)$, i.e.\ with
$A:=x(c_1)\ge1$ and $u_i:=x(c_i)/A$,
\[
  u_1=1,\qquad u_{i+1}\le2\lambda u_i-1\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i>0 .
\]
If $\lambda\le\tfrac12$ then $u_{i+1}\le u_i-1$ and $u_n\le1-(n-1)<0$ for
$n\ge3$, a contradiction; so $\lambda>\tfrac12$.  Then with
$u^\ast:=1/(2\lambda-1)$ the recursion gives
$u_i\le u^\ast-(2\lambda)^{i-1}(u^\ast-1)$, and $u_n>0$ forces
$(2\lambda)^{n-1}(u^\ast-1)<u^\ast$, that is $2(1-\lambda)(2\lambda)^{n-1}<1$.
Write $t:=1-\lambda\in(0,\tfrac12)$ and $g(t):=2t\,(2-2t)^{n-1}$, so the
condition is $g(t)<1$.  On $(0,\tfrac12]$, $g$ increases up to $t=1/n$ and
decreases after; $g(1/n)=(2/n)2^{n-1}(1-1/n)^{n-1}\ge2^{n}/(en)\ge1$ for
$n\ge5$ and $g(\tfrac12)=1$, so $g\ge1$ on $[1/n,\tfrac12]$; and for
$4\cdot2^{-n}\le t\le1/n$ one has $(1-t)^{n-1}\ge(1-1/n)^{n-1}\ge1/e$ and
hence $g(t)\ge2\cdot4\cdot2^{-n}\cdot2^{n-1}/e=4/e>1$.  Therefore
$t<4\cdot2^{-n}$.  Since $\log(1/\lambda)\le t/(1-t)<2^{-n+3}$ for
$n\ge5$, the bound of \Cref{thm:escape-class} is at least
$a\,2^{\,n-3}=2^{\Omega(N)}$.  (The exact-arithmetic feasibility test
confirms that no certificate exists at $\lambda=1-4\cdot2^{-n}$ for
$n=3,4,5$.)
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{tw:family-remark}
$M_n$ is the first family in this document that is outside all six
polynomial classes and yet provably in polynomial time: the seventh class
of \Cref{tw:modulator} contains it.  Note also that
$\val(h)=\tfrac12+2^{-(n+1)}$, so the threshold question of
\Cref{prob:main} at $v_0=h$ is decided by an exponentially small margin ---
the family is not tractable because it is coarse.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What is known, and what is not}

\begin{remark}[Literature]\label{tw:literature}
All of the following is from memory and unchecked against the sources.
Bounded treewidth is well studied for \emph{qualitative} objectives:
Obdr\v{z}\'alek proved that parity games of bounded treewidth are solved in
polynomial time, and Fearnley and Schewe sharpened the bound and its
parallel complexity; Chatterjee, {\L}\k{a}cki, Ibsen-Jensen and
Pavlogiannis give faster algorithms for Markov decision processes and
recursive state machines of constant treewidth, again for qualitative
objectives and for algebraic path properties, where the underlying problem
is already polynomial.  For the \emph{quantitative} value of a two-player
stochastic game the situation is different: the interface between two parts
of a decomposition is a vector of real numbers, not a finite type, and the
author is not aware of any polynomial or quasipolynomial algorithm for
\textsc{SSG-Value} on games of bounded treewidth in the literature.
\Cref{tw:qp} should therefore be read as new but as a candidate
rediscovery.  The two ingredients are not new: \Cref{lem:cut} is in this
document, and the \textsc{Tarski} search is
Etessami--Papadimitriou--Rubinstein--Yannakakis, who also observe that
simple stochastic games reduce to a \textsc{Tarski} fixed-point problem ---
in dimension $N$, which by itself gives nothing.  What is new is that a
decomposition lets the Tarski search be run in dimension $k+1$ at every
node of a balanced separator recursion.  For the modulator theorem the
prior art is Auger--Coucheney--Strozecki (feedback vertex number), already
recorded in this document's list; \Cref{tw:modulator} generalises the
parameter and \Cref{tw:colour-feedback} is, as far as the author knows, not
recorded.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[GAP]\label{tw:gap}
Two statements are missing.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{GAP 1.}  \emph{There is an algorithm that computes the value
vector of every stopping SSG of treewidth $k$ in time $N^{f(k)}$ for some
function $f$.}  \Cref{tw:qp} gives $N^{O(k\log N)}$; the loss is the factor
$2$ per level of the separator recursion, each level re-solving both sides
from scratch at every query.  Storing the response function instead of
re-querying it is exactly what \Cref{tw:fold-width} forbids.
\item \textbf{GAP 2.}  \emph{There is a family of stopping payoff games of
pathwidth at most $3$, with one free parameter, whose response function has
$2^{\Omega(N)}$ affine pieces.}  \Cref{tw:fold-width} achieves this at
pathwidth $4$ and \Cref{tw:one-live} forbids it at interface dimension one.
\Cref{tw:no-clock} narrows the question: a chain of identical gadgets that
read no terminal cannot fold twice, and \Cref{tw:gap2-shape} turns what
remains into a concrete one-dimensional dynamical question about
piecewise-M\"obius maps.  The heuristic against pathwidth $2$ is that a
two-dimensional interface carries an \emph{autonomous} map, while the fold
of \Cref{thm:fold} is driven by the non-autonomous constants $4^{-d}$
supplied by a third live track.
\end{itemize}
\end{remark}
